title: Sleep: The First Night Effect
main_content:
Have you ever had trouble sleeping in a new place?

Lots of people do. And now researchers from Brown University in Rhode Island think they know why.

They found that one-half of the brain “remains more awake” than the other half when people are trying to sleep in a new place.

This appears a case of the brain keeping people ready for trouble in a new place.

In their report, the researchers said many people report they have a harder time sleeping the first night at a hotel or other places outside their home.

They call it, “first-night effect.”

The researchers measured brain waves for 35 volunteers over two nights in a laboratory.

They found during the first night the left hemisphere of the brain was more active than the right hemisphere.

For some, this research may be calming. It is good to know that our brain is “looking out for us,” in a new place.

questions.question: What happens to the brain when people sleep in a new place?
options: Both hemispheres become equally active to promote sleep.
The right hemisphere becomes dominant to encourage relaxation.
The left hemisphere remains more active to maintain alertness.
The brain shuts down completely to facilitate deep sleep.
questions.answer: The left hemisphere remains more active to maintain alertness.

questions.question: What did the researchers measure?
options: Heart rates of the volunteers during sleep.
Brain waves of the volunteers during sleep.
Sleep duration of the volunteers in different locations.
The emotional responses of the volunteers to sleeping away from home.
questions.answer: Brain waves of the volunteers during sleep.
